d: (of conflict) within a group or organization
ety: Borrowed from Latin internecīnus (“deadly”), from internecium (“a massacre, bloodbath; an eradication”) + -īnus. In Latin, the sememe 'between' was here not expressed by the prefix, it instead either had a somewhat emphatic meaning or meant "down, under", comparable to its use in other Latin terms related to death: see interficiō and intereō. The English current sense is thus a reanalysis of the L
s: The Mongol people were plagued by internecine conflict until Genghis Khan unified them by focusing their aggression outwards on other peoples.

d: Appearing as such but not necessarily so
ety: Borrowed from French ostensible, formed with the suffix -ible, from Latin ostensus, the past participle of ostendō (“show”), itself from obs- (“in front of”) (akin to ob- (“in the way”)) + tendō (“stretch”) (akin to Ancient Greek τείνω (teínō)). Cf. ostentatious.
s: The ostensible reason for his visit to New York was to see his mother, but the real reason was to get to the Yankees game the next day.

d: A sudden unexpected switch
ety: From switch + -eroo.
s: The Manhattan Theater Club has pulled a switcheroo, delaying a planned production of Gone Home, by John Corwin, and replacing it with Four, by the 26-year-old playwright Christopher Shinn.

d: Having a large belly
ety: From paunch + -y.
s: He exercised every day to avoid becoming paunchy in his old age.

d: Issue an injunction
ety: From Middle English enjoinen, from Old French enjoindre (“to join with”), from Latin iniungo (“to attach”), a compound of in- (“into” “upon”) and iungo.
s: I am enjoin'd by oath to observe three things:

d: Peculiarly fortunate or appropriate; as if by divine intervention
ety: From Latin prōvidentia (“providence”) + English -al.
s: “Why, Jane,” he cried, “what do you mean? What has our providential rescue to do with altering your feelings toward me? You are but unstrung—tomorrow you will be yourself again.”

d: A stabilizer for a canoe; spars attach to a shaped log or float parallel to the hull
ety: Modification of earlier outligger after rig (“to fit out”); equivalent to out- + ligger.
s: The Sentinelese hunt in the rainforest and fish in the coastal waters using spears, bows and arrows, as well as homemade narrow outrigger canoes, according to Survival International.

d: Loud confused noise from many sources
ety: In early use, the noun is often mentioned as a cry by Irish people, and so is possibly borrowed from Irish; compare Irish ababú, abú (“used as a battle cry”), and Scottish Gaelic ub, ub, ubub (“used to express contempt, etc.”), ubh ubh (“used to express disgust”). The verb is derived from the noun.
s: The place will be in a fine hubbub, I suppose.

d: Poor enough to need help from others
ety: From Middle English indigent, from Old French indigent, from Latin indigēns, present participle of indigeō (“to need”), from indu (“in, within”) + egeō (“to be in need, want”).
s: And were I not a thing for you and me To execrate in anguish, you would be As indigent a stranger to surprise, I fear, as I was once, and as unwise.

d: Treat with excessive indulgence
ety: Probably from caudle. Compare British dialect caddle (“to coax, spoil, fondle”) and cade.
s: Let's not mollycoddle our students!

d: A hereditary ruler
ety: From Late Latin dynastēs, from Ancient Greek δυνάστης (dunástēs, “lord, ruler”), from δύναμαι (dúnamai, “to be powerful”).
s: Now the dynasts who rule each country are cementing political ties.

d: Peace of mind
ety: From Ancient Greek ἀταραξία (ataraxía), ἀ- (a-, negative prefix) + ταράσσω (tarássō, “trouble, disturb”). Doublet of ataraxy.
s: Near-synonyms: ataraxy, peace of mind, unflappability, unperturbedness

d: The form of government of a social organization
ety: From Middle French politie, from Latin polītīa, from Ancient Greek πολιτεία (politeía, “polity, policy, the state”). Doublet of police, policy, and polis (“police”).
s: New polities emerged in Europe after the fall of the Roman Empire.

d: One of the common people
ety: From Latin plēbēius (“a commoner; common”) + -an (adjective-forming suffix), from Latin plēbēs + -ius (adjective-forming suffix), possibly under the influence of Middle French plebeyen, plebein, plebien (“a commoner”) and plebeien (“concerning the common people”). Cf. Medieval Latin plēbēiānus (“a commoner”), from plēbēius + -ānus.
s: The cognomen was first used in patrician families, who were distinguished from the plebeians by their three names.

d: Coinciding with reality
ety: From Latin veridicus (“truly said”), from verus (“true”) and dīcō (“to say”).
s: Few believe that all claimed religious experiences are veridical.

d: A long and mournful complaint
ety: From French jérémiade, from Jérémie, from Latin Ieremias, from Hebrew ירמיה (yirm'yá, “Jeremiah”). Named after biblical prophet Jeremiah, who lamented the moral state of Judah and predicted her downfall.
s: “This is precisely the manner of Balkanization that Schlesinger cautioned us about in his prescient jeremiad on multiculturalism, “The Disuniting of America.””

d: Lacking intelligence and vitality
ety: From dialectal English gaum (“heed, attention”) + -less (“without”), from Old Norse gaum, from Proto-Germanic *gaumaz, *gaumō (“heed, attention”). The ‘r’ found in this spelling is a vowel-lengthening device common in non-rhotic dialects of English.
s: Did I ever look so stupid: so gormless as Joseph calls it?

d: (of the feet of water birds) having three toes connected by a thin fold of skin
ety: Learned borrowing from Latin palmātus (“hand-shaped, palm-leaf shaped”), from palma (“palm, palm-tree”). Equivalent to palm + -ate (adjective-forming suffix). Compare French palmé.
s: Although palmate leaves are typical of most Western maples, a number of species have leaves without lobes.

d: A political leader who seeks support by appealing to popular passions and prejudices
ety: From Middle French démagogue, from Ancient Greek δημαγωγός (dēmagōgós, “popular leader, mob leader”), from δῆμος (dêmos, “people”) + ἀγωγός (agōgós, “guide”). By surface analysis, dem- + -agogue.
s: 1938, O'Neill, translating The Knights by Aristophanes, 424 BC, lines 191-193, A demagogue must be neither an educated nor an honest man; he has to be an ignoramus and a rogue.

d: Having a smooth or slippery quality
ety: Learned borrowing from Latin lūbricus (“slippery”). Doublet of lubricous.
s: Lubricious bank managers and building society chairmen who have never danced before throw off their jackets, confess to barren lives and worship Rick the giver of their sun and rain.

d: Steal goods; take as spoils
ety: From Middle English despoylen, dispoylen, from Old French despoillier ( > French dépouiller), from Latin dēspoliō, dēspoliāre.
s: They've come to witness the Beginning. The rebirth of Paradise, despoiled by mankind.

d: Cause to seem less serious; play down
ety: Derived from Latin dēnigrātus, the perfect passive participle of dēnigrō (“to blacken”) [see -ate (verb-forming suffix)], from dē- (“of; from”) + nigrō (“to blacken”) [from niger (“black”)]. Cognate with Middle English denigart(e) (“darkened, discolored”).
s: You have no right to denigrate people and things that you have no personal experience with.

d: A corrupt or depraved or degenerate act or practice
ety: Borrowed from Middle French turpitude, from Latin turpitūdō (“baseness, infamy”), from turpis (“foul, base”).
s: As for the moral turpitude that man unveiled to me, even with tears of penitence, I cannot, even in memory, dwell on it without a start of horror.

d: Reverent petition to a deity
ety: From Middle English orisoun, from Anglo-Norman oreison, oresoun etc. and Old French oraisun etc., from Latin ōrātiō, ōrātiōnem (“discourse, prayer”) (whence also English oration).
s: ‘Pass on, pass on, don’t interrupt the hermit at his orisons.’

d: A very intense and uncontrolled fire
ety: From Middle French, from Latin cōnflagrātiō (“burning, conflagration”).
s: It took sixty firefighters to put out the conflagration.

d: Become of; happen to
ety: From Middle English bityden [and other forms]; from bi- (prefix forming verbs, usually with a completive, figurative, or intensive sense) + tyden (“to come about, happen, occur; to befall, become of, happen to (someone); to be the fate of (someone); to await (someone); to fare, get along”); tyden is derived from Old English tīdan (“to befall, betide, happen”), related to tīd (“time; season; hour”)
s: Whether good or ill betide you, trust in yourself.

d: A hoop worn beneath a skirt to extend it horizontally; worn by European women in the 16th and 17th centuries
ety: Hobson-Jobson of earlier forms vardingale, etc., borrowed from Middle French verdugale, from Spanish verdugado, from verdugo (“rod”).
s: In Henry VIII's Great Hall, there were men in doublets and codpieces prancing up and down with women in farthingales.

d: Portico at the west end of an early Christian basilica or church
ety: From Ancient Greek νάρθηξ (nárthēx, “giant fennel; casket”), a Pre-Greek word, as suggested by the suffix. See also νάρδος (nárdos, “nard”).
s: “Cinco,” Marco bellowed now, hurrying across the narthex to give him a hearty handshake, which Cinco returned without enthusiasm.

d: Make plain and comprehensible
ety: Borrowed from Latin explicāre (“unfold, explain”).
s: My homework is to explicate a poem.

d: Not liable to error
ety: From in- + errant.
s: He questions the tenability of regarding the Scriptures as inerrant, since no original copies exist.

d: A strap from the back of a saddle passing under the horse’s tail; prevents saddle from slipping forward
ety: From Middle English croper, crouper, from Anglo-Norman cruper, cropere, from Old French cropiere, crupiere, from the same Germanic root as croup. Doublet of croupiere.
s: Our knight did bear no less a pack / Of his own buttocks on his back: / Which now had almost got the upper- / Hand of his head, for want of crupper.

d: Of a mental act performed entirely within the mind
ety: Entered English around 1530, via French, from Late Latin immanēns, present participle of Latin immanēre, from im- (“in”) + manēre (“to dwell, remain, stay”). Cognate with remain and manor.
s: At the same time he was convinced of the complete immanent presence of God in history, and rejected whatever remained in Hegelianism of the notion of a personal God.

d: Charming in a childlike or naive way
ety: Inherited from Middle English wynsom, winsom, winsome, winsum, wunsum (“beautiful; agreeable, gracious, pleasant; generous; of situations: favourable, propitious”), from Old English wynsum (“joyful, merry, pleasant; winsome”), from Proto-West Germanic *wunnjusam (“joyful”). By surface analysis, winne (“delight, joy, pleasure”) + -some.
s: “We have to begin to step up and communicate this message in ways that are winsome and compelling,” he added.

d: A long brightly colored shawl; worn mainly by Mexican men
ety: Borrowed from Mexican Spanish serape.
s: Could be, said John Grady. He took off his hat and lay back and pulled the serape over him.

d: A musical phrase repeated over and over during a composition
ety: From Italian ostinato (“stubborn”). Doublet of obstinate.
s: The piece moves in alluring spans of swirling figures, jagged lines and pointillistic outbursts, often prodded forward by ostinatos in the perky piano.

d: A pedestrian who walks from place to place
ety: From Middle English weyfarere, weifarere; equivalent to way + farer.
s: His head far down the hot sweet throat of her — So one tracks love, whose breath is deadlier, And lo, one springe and you are fast in hell, Fast as the gin's grip of a wayfarer.

d: A vain and talkative person (chatters like a parrot)
ety: From Middle English popinjay, popyngeay, popingay, popejay, from Anglo-Norman papegai, papejoie et al., (northern) Old French papejai (“parrot”), probably from Old Occitan papagay (compare Occitan papagai, Catalan papagai), ultimately from Arabic بَبْغَاء (babḡāʔ, “parrot”), of imitative origin.
s: The very quintessence of popinjay vulgarity is reached when nicely is made to do service for well, in this wise: "How do you do?" "Nicely." "How are you?" "Nicely."

d: Not worth using
ety: From Middle French inutile, from Latin inutilis. Philippine usage is likely from Tagalog inutil, from Spanish inútil, from the same source. By surface analysis, in- + utile.
s: He had already demanded the attention of the manager, Professor Bulge, Draycott and two underlings to his case and they were now involved in a babel of inutile reiteration.

d: Distasteful and unpleasant; spoiled by mixture
ety: From Scottish brack (from Middle Dutch brac (“brackish”)) + -ish. Cognate with Dutch brak (“brackish”), German Low German brack, brakerg, brakig (“brackish”), German brackig (“brackish”), Danish brak (“brackish”), Swedish bräck (“brackish”), Norwegian brakk (“brackish”). Perhaps a distant doublet of brook.
s: Therefore the bread he had to eat Seemed brackish, less like corn than tares;

d: Loud and resounding
ety: From Latin plangēns, present participle of plangō (“to beat; to lament”).
s: Since mid-day their plangent, disquieting cries had foretold its approach.
